phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar fricative [s], as in English 'sun'.
Voiced dental [t], rolled or tapped r, short [i]; the element's root is opaque.
Voiced bilabial [b], open-mid back [ɔ], voiced velar [ɡ] — the element *bogъ, 'god', shared with Dažbog.

pronunciation.approximation: 'STREE-bog', rolled r, stress forward; the second half of the name literally means 'god'.

kin.label: Common Slavic
kin.form: *Stribogъ — the second element is *bogъ 'god' (compare Dažbog, 'giving god'); the first element is opaque

kin.label: Proposals
kin.form: connections with roots meaning 'arrow' and 'to spread, scatter' circulate in the literature; none commands consensus (Gieysztor; Brückner)

kin.label: Epic genealogy
kin.form: the Slovo o polku Igoreve gives him a family anyway: the winds are 'grandsons of Stribog'

pronunciation.note: Tier 2. The restored form Stribog preserves no feature the plain ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive non-ASCII letter — so the temple stands at Tier 2 by the mechanical rule. The gloss 'father of winds' is traditional; the name's deeper etymology is not settled.

domains.title: Stribog
domains.subtitle: Winds
domains.lead: Stribog is the wind-god of the Kyiv pantheon, sixth of the six idols cast into the Dnieper in 988. His name's second element is the word for 'god'; its first is opaque — but the epic tradition calls the winds his grandsons, and that one formula is the whole of his surviving theology.

cards.name: The Winds
cards.desc: His domain by every ancient inference: the moving air that brings thaw, storm, and war-weather.

cards.name: Grandfather of Winds
cards.desc: The Slovo o polku Igoreve calls the winds 'grandsons of Stribog' — a complete genealogy in one phrase.

cards.name: Sixth of the Six
cards.desc: Listed among the idols of Kyiv in the Primary Chronicle: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, Mokosh.

cards.name: The Opaque Name
cards.desc: No other god's name so resists analysis; its first element is an open problem of Slavic philology.

symbols.name: Wind and weather
symbols.meaning: The element itself, which the epic makes his family: the winds do what grandsons do

symbols.name: Storm cloud and squall
symbols.meaning: The war-weather of the Slovo — the black sky under which Igor's campaign marched

symbols.name: The steppe horizon
symbols.meaning: Kyiv's winds came off the open steppe; his one vivid scene is a steppe wind rising from the sea

symbols.name: The moving air of thaw
symbols.meaning: The spring winds that break the river ice — function inferred from his wind-kin, not attested

mythology.lead: The sources for Stribog are two lines long: a place in the chronicle's list of drowned idols, and a genealogy in the nation's greatest poem. Everything else — his character, his rites, his season — is inference, and this entry says so wherever inference is doing the work.

myths.title: The Idols in the Dnieper
myths.text: When Vladimir's baptism swept the old pantheon into the Dnieper in 988, the Primary Chronicle preserved the full list of the drowned: Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh. No anecdote attaches to Stribog — no oath, no sorcerer, no gloss, no weeping crowd. Of the six he is the most silent: not first like Perun, not glossed like Dažbog, not folk-remembered like Mokosh. Yet the chronicler's list is itself a kind of myth — the orderly procession of gods into the river, each name checked off as it sinks, is the Christian founding story of Rus', and Stribog's place in that procession is the entire record of his worship. A god can be a major power and still leave no story; the river took his narrative along with his statue, and the list is the wake.

myths.title: The Grandsons of Stribog
myths.text: The single vivid sentence about Stribog stands in the Slovo o polku Igoreve (c. 1185), the greatest work of Old Rus' literature. As Igor's doomed army rides out against the Polovtsians, the poet summons the omens, and the winds rise on cue: 'Then the winds, Stribog's grandsons, blew from the sea' — a squall driving the dust and the portents before it. The phrase is a fossil of theology. Where a monk would write 'God sent a storm,' the epic poet instinctively reaches for kinship: the winds are not Stribog's subjects or his weapons but his grandsons, doing what grandsons do — arriving uninvited, raising a racket, unmistakably of the family. Two centuries after the idols sank, the grammar of the old pantheon still blew through the language like weather that knows its own name.

myths.title: The Name That Won't Decode
myths.text: Everything else about Stribog is a problem on a philologist's desk. The second half of the name is *bogъ, 'god' — the same element that gives us Dažbog, 'giving god' — but the first half, *strib-, has no agreed root. Comparisons with words for 'arrow' and for 'spreading' or 'scattering' have circulated in the literature for a century; none carries the field, and even the vowel of the name wavers in the manuscript tradition. Some scholars have wondered whether the first element is not Slavic at all — a loan like the Iranian Simurgh behind Simargl — though no convincing donor language has stepped forward. The handbooks (Gieysztor; Brückner) state the honest position plainly: we hold the god's name, a wind-function inferred from one epic line, and nothing else. A whole deity, reduced to one sentence and an unsolved etymology.

myths.title: What the Sources Do Not Say
myths.text: It is worth stating plainly what the tradition does not contain, because Stribog is the clearest case of a god known by structure rather than by story. No chronicle puts a curse in his mouth; no treaty swears by him; no saint inherits his day; no festival, icon, or temple is recorded; and no folk song or charm preserves his name past the Middle Ages. His rank — sixth of the six gods of the capital — implies a cult of real standing; his total silence implies that the sources which would have given him a biography either never existed or did not survive. Modern Slavic Native Faith has had to invent his feast-day, his attributes, and his character outright — a revealing anachronism, since Stribog today is exactly what a wind-god would be if reconstructed from the bare name alone. The scholarship knows the limits, and says so; the temple should too.

lore.syncretism: Stribog attracted no Christian successor — no saint took the winds from him the way Elijah took Perun's storm — and Byzantine writers had no classical slot for a wind-god, so no interpretatio rescued him either. His afterlife is purely literary and comparative. Comparative mythology seats him beside the Vedic Vāyu, master of the winds, and beside the Greek winds as a brood rather than a person — Aeolus managing his bag of quarrelsome grandchildren. In the twentieth century Rodnover calendars promoted him as a god of winds and weather, roles extrapolated from the Slovo formula; fantasy fiction and games drift him as a stock 'old Slavic' name. The most honest syncretism is the one the poet performed unwittingly: naming the winds a family. That is how a polytheist sky is actually experienced — every gust somebody's relative, every storm a household arriving.
lore.culturalLegacy: Stribog's legacy is almost entirely onomastic and literary. The Slovo's phrase 'Stribog's grandsons' entered every anthology of Old Rus' literature and every schoolroom, so that his name survives more widely read than those of gods with far richer cults. Modern paganism adopted him enthusiastically but thinly: he appears in Rodnover calendars and in fantasy fiction, games, and brand names, usually as a generic wind or storm patron — attributes supplied by authors, not sources. For linguists he remains a standing exhibit in seminars on Slavic theonymy, a name whose opaque first element defeats each new generation of etymologists. If Perun is the god who would not die and Veles the god who would not stay hidden, Stribog is the god who never quite existed in the record — a place kept for the wind in the pantheon's seating plan, honored now mostly by being quoted correctly.
lore.extendedMeditation: Stribog is the god of what passes through. Wind cannot be sworn by, cannot be fed, cannot even be consistently blamed — and so the tradition left him almost nothing to hold. What the epic gives him instead is better than a cult: a family. The winds are his grandsons — not his subjects, not his weapons, his grandsons, the way weather actually behaves, arriving uninvited, full of intentions, unmistakably related. The phrase is a miniature of how polytheism worked before it learned to be systematic: the world is not governed, it is inhabited, by beings with kin. Stribog matters to the modern imagination precisely because he is so nearly empty — a vessel into which every age pours its theory of the wind, from philology's unsolved root to fantasy's storm lord. Perhaps a god who is only a name and a family of winds is the truest wind-god of all: felt everywhere, pinned down nowhere, and quoted — 'the winds, Stribog's grandsons' — whenever the air itself needs a lineage.
lore.archaeology: No artifact, building, image, or inscription can be tied to Stribog. Unlike Perun's Peryn' enclosure or Veles's Novgorod street, the wind-god left no footprint in the ground, and the destruction of 988 swept away whatever shrine the Kyiv hill may have held. Wind and storm imagery on medieval jewelry and amulets — whirlwind stamps, storm-bird pendants — is sometimes laid at his door, but the attributions are decorative rather than demonstrated, and nothing bears his name. The Slovo's 'grandsons of Stribog' remains his only monument: a line of verse that has outlasted every temple in the pantheon, copied in more than a hundred manuscripts of the national epic and read aloud in classrooms eight centuries after the last wind was officially his.
